questions.q: What does this lesson say is the misconception about accessing Salesforce through the API versus the UI?
options: That the API is a separate, looser security context -- in reality it inherits the same object- and field-level access the logged-in user already has
That the API requires a stronger password than the UI
That the UI is faster than the API for bulk data access
That the API cannot be used by integration users at all
questions.explain: Salesforce's API enforces the same profile- and permission-set-based object and field access as the UI -- there is no separate, looser rulebook for API calls.

questions.q: What does the 'API Enabled' permission actually do?
options: It automatically disables UI login for that user
It grants a user unlimited access to every object regardless of their profile
It only applies to Chatter-related API calls
It is a required gate -- without it, API calls fail entirely regardless of the user's other object/field access
questions.explain: API Enabled is a precondition: a user needs it before making any API call at all. Having it doesn't grant extra access -- it's the gate that must be open before the user's existing object/field/record access becomes usable through the API.

questions.q: What does the 'API Only User' profile setting do?
options: It increases the user's API call volume limit
It grants the user access to every object without a permission set
It blocks that user from logging in through the standard UI at all, while still permitting API access
It disables TLS enforcement for that user's connections
questions.explain: API Only closes off one avenue of misuse for a compromised integration credential -- it can't be used to simply log into the Salesforce UI and browse around, even though API access still works.

questions.q: How does an OAuth scope relate to the underlying user's permissions, per this lesson?
options: A scope can grant access beyond what the user's profile and permission sets allow
Scopes have no effect at all on API access
Scopes only apply to the Authorization Code flow, never to any other OAuth flow
A scope narrows what a given token can be used for; it never widens access past what the underlying identity's permissions already allow
questions.explain: OAuth scope is a second, narrower filter layered on top of the user's existing access -- it restricts what a token can be used for, but an overly broad scope on an over-privileged user still leaves that user over-privileged.

questions.q: What transport-layer requirement does this lesson say Salesforce enforces automatically for every API connection?
options: A minimum of three-factor authentication
A mandatory VPN tunnel for every API call
TLS, with a minimum cipher key-length requirement and no unencrypted fallback
A maximum of one API call per minute per user
questions.explain: Salesforce requires TLS for API connections (with a minimum cipher strength) as a platform-enforced baseline -- an integration that can't negotiate a current TLS version simply cannot connect, with no weaker fallback available.
